label: Hooked, tickets, winning
rationale: What comes up once a hobby takes hold: being into something right now, managing to get tickets for a concert or game, and a match won or lost.
mixUps: geemu ni hamaru and shiai ni katsu both take ni where English uses 'into' or a direct object, never o. chiketto o toru keeps o, and its toru means securing them (toreta! = I got them), not buying (katta) or being given them (moratta).

targets.english: be hooked on games; be really into games
targets.verbSense: fit snugly into, get stuck in; hence get hooked on
targets.trap: English has no verb for being into something, so learners fall back on suki desu. suki is fine but only says you like it in general; for a current craze natives say X ni hamatteru, with ni, never o.
targets.use: Use it for what you are into right now. It is almost always hamatteru (am hooked), as in saikin X ni hamatteru; hamatta means got hooked. It works with any hobby.
targets.notes: Colloquial but mainstream (dictionaries mark this sense as slang, and the katakana shows it): fine in casual and friendly polite talk; in a formal setting say X ni kyoumi ga arimasu. Milder: X ni kyoumi ga aru (interested in). Stronger: X ni muchuu ni natteru (completely absorbed in). hamatta also means got stuck: juutai ni hamatta (got stuck in traffic).

example.ja: 最近このゲームにハマってる
example.english: I'm hooked on this game lately.

examplePolite.ja: 最近このゲームにハマってます
examplePolite.english: I've been hooked on this game lately.

targets.verbSense: win; beat (both the contest and the opponent take ni)
targets.trap: Not shiai o katsu: English 'win the game' takes an object, but Japanese wins at it with ni. shiai de katsu (win in the match) is also fine. The same ni marks who you beat: Kankoku ni katta = we beat Korea (not Kankoku o).
targets.use: Use it about any match or game you played or watched. It is mostly past tense (katta, or kateta for managed to win). In speech the match is usually said first as the topic and katta stands alone (kinou no shiai, katta yo). Keep ni when the match follows straight on: shiai ni katta.
targets.notes: English 'win' is wider: win a prize = shou o morau / toru; win the lottery = takarakuji ga ataru.

examplePolite.romaji: kinou no shiai ni kachimashita yo
examplePolite.ja: 昨日の試合に勝ちましたよ

targets.trap: Not shiai o nakusu: nakusu is losing an object. A contest is makeru with ni, never o; shiai de makeru is also fine. The same ni marks who beat you: Kankoku ni maketa = we lost to Korea.
targets.use: It is mostly past tense: maketa, or makechatta (lost, sadly; makechaimashita among colleagues). In speech the match is usually said first as the topic (kinou no shiai, makechatta), and the team goes unsaid. Otherwise keep ni: shiai ni maketa.

example.ja: 昨日の試合、負けちゃった

examplePolite.ja: 昨日の試合に負けました

targets.verbSense: take; also get hold of, secure (seats, bookings, rooms)
targets.trap: Not chiketto o morau, which means someone gave them to you: tickets you secure yourself are toru (kau, buy, is also fine), and 'I got them!' is toreta! (casually also getto shita!).
targets.use: Said about securing tickets for concerts, games, flights or the shinkansen, often ones that sell out. You hear the can-form toreru most, which takes ga (usually dropped in speech): chiketto toreta! (got them!), torenakatta (couldn't get any).
targets.notes: kippu is a train ticket (kippu o kau); for the shinkansen you hear both. chiketto covers concerts, games, flights and anything booked online.

example.ja: ライブのチケット取れた！
example.english: I got tickets for the concert!

examplePolite.ja: ライブのチケットが取れました！
examplePolite.english: I got tickets for the concert!

reviewPool.english: take time off work, miss work
